title: The Prophet Motive
author: Ashman, Greg
summary: The author revisits Andy Hargreaves's 2011 foreword to Pasi Sahlberg's Finnish Lessons after a public dispute with Hargreaves over interpreting the 2025 PISA results, arguing that both men have a long track record of being wrong about what drives national education outcomes while facing no professional consequences for it. He recounts predicting Finland's PISA decline back in the early 2010s, contrary to the foreword's celebration of Finland's teacher autonomy, master's-level teacher training, and decentralized curriculum as the drivers of its earlier success, success that, per other researchers cited, was actually achieved by cohorts educated under Finland's older, more centralized and traditional system. He criticizes Hargreaves's newer claim that England's strong PISA results must reflect either sampling problems or teachers secretly abandoning explicit instruction, calling it evidence of extreme bias against explicit teaching rather than a serious methodological critique. The piece closes by generalizing the complaint: prominent education 'prophets' who champion Finland-style reforms can be repeatedly wrong about outcomes and still be feted with professorships and paid speaking engagements, because unlike in engineering, failure in education policy is neither obvious nor immediate.
points: Check the 'direction of travel' in international test data, not just single-year rankings, before drawing conclusions about which education systems are succeeding.

Distinguish causal claims about Finland's earlier PISA success from the more progressive reforms Finland pursued afterward, since the successful cohort was educated under the older, more traditional system.
Be skeptical of experts who dismiss unfavorable results as sampling artifacts or 'subversive' teaching rather than engaging with the substance.
Note the incentive mismatch: education commentators who are repeatedly wrong about system-level outcomes often face no professional cost, unlike fields where failure is immediate and visible.
quotes: I have never been convinced by rankings and my first look is always to the direction of travel.

Hargreaves seems to claim that students simply cannot be prepared for PISA questions through explicit teaching and so if England’s scores turn out to be correct, it must be because subversive teachers are side-stepping explicit teaching.
Whatever China, Singapore, Finland or anywhere else is starting to do now, it cannot possibly be the cause of past successes.
Given that Finland’s PISA successes in the early 2000s were with fifteen-year-olds still educated under the older system, this argument fits the data.
there are figures in education, such as Hargreaves, Yong Zhao and Pasi Sahlberg, with long histories of being wrong and yet this appears to come at no professional cost.
being right is not a strategy and certainly not a requirement for any aspiring prophet of education.
